searchText: the idea is that the old-style contract would interpret `msg.sender` as being the compressed address So the old-style contract would save the balance at the storage slot corresponding to the compressed address And allow transfers out when the msg.sender equals the compressed address Yes, msg.sender is the compressed one. But due to ABI encoding, any target address submitted by the user would be truncated to 160-bits. So either they can only token transfer to old-style addresses, or new-style addresses which already exists in the translation table. So basically, addresses coming in to old-style addresses are compressed, and then calls coming out of old-style addresses are decompressed Yes, that's true And unavoidable You'd need a wrapper contract to properly support new addresses So a simple solution maybe having that "add me to the translation table" feature 🙂 hmm technically you could just make a contract that just immediately does a call to the msg.sender So such a feature exists automatically Yes, that's what I mentioned above. Just having a single such contract may be better then people making up new ones for it. sure, we can make a recommended contract, or even hard-fork one into some address actually, something like extbalance would be a simpler one to poke the table, wouldn't it be? yep So a wrapper could be just doing an extbalance and then invoking the token contract. sorry I am just a lurker, but could you solve the "old style addresses coming out" to have a "magic padding" for old style addresses that the system understands means ignore the "new bits" because this address is smaller? right but in the long term, moving to more than 80 bits of security is better that's kinda what my proposal does, in that a new-style address must be >= 2**160 So it can't be in the same space as old-style addresses so if an old address is 4 bytes and a new one is 8 bytes your proposal says say if you see FF FF XX XX then ignore the FF FF and use the last 4 bytes only? But any other initial value for the first 4 bytes is fair game? again sorry just getting up to speed If you have a contract that accepts 32-byte addresses and you see an address that starts with enough zeroes, then you know it's old style You can't really make compressed addresses "special", because the entire 2**160 space is already taken up okay cool, (FF or 00 doesn't really matter to me) you are expanding the address size though right? People are lazy, if it is possible to use wrappers, they will. It should be disincentivized by making accessing the translation table expensive. yeah the whole point here is to expand the address size from 20 to 32 bytes And it will be It would require a whole witness read so why stop at 32bytes? why not add some bytes that you can stuff with a "version" 32 bytes is the size of a "chunk"; it becomes logistically much harder to expand beyond 32 bytes And also once you get above 100 bits of security (which you get at 25 bytes) there's little value in going further Yes, in the state expiry model. Though here you wanted to black box it, so theoretically speaking adding this on current mainnet, one would just need to make old-style poking have an extra charge 🙂 I mean you only need 1 byte, but to make it 16 byte or 32 byte aligned take more if that makes sense most protocols "save" a byte at the front, say for version then you can make these switches or some other switch easier in the future right, that's what my proposal does ^^ fair enough Only supporting two byte immediate jumps makes bytecode manipulation easier. That way you don't have to switch between short jump and long jump when you change the code size. Right. Making the jump locations themselves dependent on bytecode makes the algorithm to actually calculate the jumpdests sequential in an annoying way As earlier jumpdest values would affect later ones, so you can have cascades Still doable in linear time, but very annoying Also, relative jumps are easier than absolute jumps. Though, having a jump table may be easier than either. Related: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2677 -- I think we should try to get this in if any more advanced form of jumpdest analysis is on the table in the future.
